strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: grounding automatic tool creation in external reference materials to extend LLM capabilities beyond internal knowledge, which is a meaningful and underexplored direction relative to prior work (CREATOR, LATM, Trove).

Comprehensive evaluation across three distinct domains (causality, physics, chemistry), four utilization LLMs, and multiple baseline families (PoT/ReAct, RAG, general tool creation, domain-specific methods), making the comparison reasonably fair and thorough.

Thoughtful ablations that isolate the two key components: code-form tools vs. raw text (Hierarchical RAG) and hierarchical selection vs. similarity retrieval, supporting the paper's central design claims.

Additional analyses strengthen the contribution: human evaluation of tool quality and human-model selection consistency, cost analysis showing large efficiency gains over ChemAgent/Physics Reasoner, robustness to alternative tool-creation models, o1-mini compatibility, and cross-dataset tool reuse on SciBench-fund.
The paper is well written with a clear two-module framework, and appendices provide prompts, implementation details, and per-sub-dataset results supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The evaluation setup embeds a non-trivial oracle assumption: the reference textbook must be chosen to match the evaluation domain by a knowledgeable human. In practice, selecting the right book is a substantial part of the problem, and the paper gives little analysis of robustness when references are suboptimal, noisy, or partially mismatched.

Dataset sizes are small (e.g., 114 physics, 118 chemistry, 269 causality questions), and many headline margins are modest (e.g., 57.7 vs. 56.3 for ChemAgent on chemistry; 41.6 vs. 43.8 for ReAct+RefTool vs. ReAct on causality under ReAct). No statistical significance testing or variance analysis over repeated runs is reported, so several claimed gains may not be reliable.

Excluding baselines from the main tables based on preliminary underperformance (ReAct for physics/chemistry, CoT/direct reasoning) somewhat weakens the strength of the comparisons; ChemAgent, the closest competitor in chemistry, relies on a different operating regime (validation-time trial-and-error) that may not be a like-for-like cost comparison.

There is a potential knowledge-leakage confound: the tool-creation model (GPT-4o/Gemini) likely already has internalized much of these well-known textbooks, so the gains may partly reflect better-structured elicitation of internal knowledge rather than truly extending beyond it; the paper's central claim of overcoming knowledge limitations is not directly tested on genuinely novel or post-training-cutoff material.

Novelty is moderate: the framework is largely a pipeline combining LLM-based code generation, execution-based filtering (standard practice), and structure-guided retrieval (similar in spirit to AnyTool's hierarchical API selection); each component is individually well known.

Some inconsistencies and presentation issues: the abstract's 'Code is in' sentence is incomplete; improvements vary considerably across models and domains (RefTool hurts vs. PoT for GPT-4 in the causality ablation), and the chemistry hyperparameters were tuned on SciBench validation data while other domains used defaults, complicating cross-domain comparability.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the framework (reference-guided tool creation + hierarchical tool selection) is well-motivated: grounding tool generation in textbooks is a sensible way to extend tool creation beyond LLMs' internal knowledge.

Evaluation spans three domains (causality, physics, chemistry), four utilization LLMs, and a diverse set of baselines (PoT, ReAct, RAG with the same books, Creator, and domain-specific methods), which is more thorough than typical.

The paper includes useful analyses: ablations separating tool representation from hierarchical selection, human evaluation of tool quality and selection consistency, cost analysis, tool reusability on a held-out dataset, and robustness to an alternative tool-creation model.
The cost analysis (Table 5) convincingly shows the method is far cheaper than trial-and-error alternatives like ChemAgent, supporting the practicality claim.
Prompt templates, evaluation protocol details, and limitations are documented in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core recipe is 'prompt an LLM to write Python functions from textbook sections, validate by execution, and retrieve via the book's table of contents.' Each ingredient (LLM tool synthesis, execution-based filtering, hierarchy-guided retrieval as in AnyTool) is established; the contribution is a straightforward combination, and the paper overstates it as a new paradigm.

Gains are inconsistent and often small. In causality, ReAct+RefTool improves over ReAct by only 2.5% on average, and for GPT-4 the PoT+RefTool gain is modest. In the ablation (Table 4), hierarchical selection actually hurts GPT-4 on causality (38.7 vs. 46.1 for similarity-based selection), which undercuts the claimed advantage of hierarchical retrieval. The headline 11.3% average improvement masks this heterogeneity, and no statistical significance tests are reported anywhere.

Some evaluation choices weaken fairness: (1) for chemistry, hyperparameters (nc, nt) are grid-searched on the SciBench validation set, while other domains use defaults without validation—baselines did not receive equivalent tuning; (2) the 'atkins' SciBench subset is excluded due to overlap with the reference book, which raises data-contamination concerns about the remaining chemistry subsets (drawn from textbook exercises of similar sources) that are not adequately addressed; (3) CoT/direct baselines are relegated to the appendix with per-benchmark justifications.

The human evaluation is small (20 tools and 20 questions per domain, apparently a single annotator) and the 'consistency with humans' metric conditions on cases where both human and model select tools, introducing selection bias; the claimed 3.3% advantage of hierarchical over similarity-based retrieval rests on limited evidence with domain-dependent reversals.

Reference material selection is effectively manual and oracle-like: the authors hand-pick the textbook matching each benchmark's domain. The paper claims generalizability, but there is no experiment on selecting references automatically or on performance when the chosen reference is only partially relevant, so the 'broadly generalizable' claim is stronger than the evidence.

Missing comparisons and details: no comparison with full-length-book prompting (e.g., Gemini-1.5-Pro's 1M+ context could simply ingest the entire textbook, a natural and cheap baseline for the RAG comparison); no error bars or variance estimates despite small test sets (e.g., 71–118 questions); the tool-creation cost in Table 5 is reported only for physics and chemistry, and GPU usage (8x A800) is mentioned without explaining what it is used for.

Polish issues: the abstract ends with an incomplete sentence ('Code is in'), and several claims (e.g., 'cost-efficient and broadly generalizable') are repeated without additional supporting experiments.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: grounding automatic tool creation in structured external references (textbooks) rather than the LLM's internal knowledge, which plausibly extends tool creation to domains beyond the model's knowledge scope; the hierarchical toolbox mirroring the reference structure is a natural and elegant design choice.

Comprehensive evaluation: three domains (causality, physics, chemistry), four strong LLMs for tool utilization, plus additional experiments on a reasoning model (o1-mini), an alternative tool-creation model (Gemini-1.5-Pro), and a held-out dataset (SciBench-fund) to demonstrate tool reusability.

Well-designed baselines and ablations: the comparison against RAG using the *same* reference books is a particularly important control that isolates the benefit of the tool representation and hierarchical selection; the ablation study cleanly disentangles code-form tools vs. raw text and hierarchical vs. similarity-based selection (1.9% and 2.6% average gains respectively).

Good analyses beyond headline numbers: human evaluation of tool faithfulness/correctness/usefulness, human-model agreement on tool selection, cost/time analysis showing large efficiency advantages over ChemAgent and Physics Reasoner, and illustrative case studies.

Reasonably transparent: implementation details, prompts, evaluation protocols, and a limitations section are provided; exclusion of certain baselines (e.g., methods using training data or web search) is justified.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the framework is a combination of known techniques (LLM tool generation, execution-based filtering as in Trove/CRAFT-style work, hierarchical retrieval as in AnyTool) applied in a new configuration; the conceptual contribution is useful but not groundbreaking.

The key assumption is underexamined: the method presupposes that a suitable, domain-matched reference book is available and correctly selected by a human. This is a nontrivial hidden human cost, and the paper does not discuss or test what happens with imperfect/mismatched references, nor the cost of converting books to LaTeX.

Tool validation relies on self-generated examples: the expected answers used for output verification come from the LLM itself, so a systematically wrong model can validate an incorrectly implemented tool (execution testing alone cannot catch faithfulness errors). The human evaluation partially mitigates this but is small in scale (20 tools per domain, apparently a single expert annotator per domain, no inter-annotator agreement reported).

Gains over the strongest baselines are modest and inconsistent: the headline 11.3% average improvement is largely driven by the weak Creator baseline; compared to plain PoT/ReAct, improvements are roughly 2-5%, and in some configurations RefTool underperforms (e.g., GPT-4 on chemistry: PoT+RAG 54.1 vs. PoT+RefTool 53.4; Gemini-created tools are strictly worse than GPT-4o-created ones on physics). No statistical significance tests are reported for the small evaluation sets (e.g., 114 physics questions, 71 SciBench-fund questions).

Some evidence of sensitivity and cherry-picking risk: hyperparameters (nc, nt) are grid-searched on the SciBench validation set only for chemistry, while defaults are used elsewhere; subsets of SciBench-physics and the 'atkins' chemistry sub-dataset are excluded, which—though justified—narrows the evaluation scope; the small o1-mini experiment is labeled small-scale without details.

Minor presentation issues: the abstract's 'Code is in' sentence is incomplete (broken code link); per-section tool cap (m=2) and prompt design choices appear somewhat ad hoc; the related-work comparison to AnyTool (hierarchical API selection) could be more deeply differentiated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: grounding automatic tool creation in external references rather than LLM internal knowledge is a sensible and useful direction for knowledge-intensive domains.

Comprehensive evaluation across three scientific domains (causality, physics, chemistry) and four base LLMs, with appropriate baselines spanning general reasoning, RAG, tool-creation methods, and domain-specific reasoners.

Strong and thorough analyses: ablations separating the contribution of code-form tools vs. hierarchical selection, cost/time analysis, human evaluation of tool quality (faithfulness, correctness, usefulness), human-LLM tool selection consistency study, robustness to alternative tool-creation models, and comparison against continued pretraining/fine-tuning on the same reference material (Table 8), which strengthens the core claim that tools are a better knowledge transfer mechanism than direct training.

Demonstrated generalization beyond scientific tasks: applying the framework to extremely low-resource language translation with unstructured grammar rules is a convincing out-of-domain test, and tool reusability across datasets (SciBench-fund) supports the dataset-agnostic claim.
Good practical efficiency: tool creation cost is amortized and inference is much cheaper than trial-and-error methods like ChemAgent; code and data release supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the core idea (convert reference material into executable code tools, validate, organize hierarchically) is a fairly natural combination of existing ingredients (tool creation à la LATM/Creator/TroVE, hierarchical API organization à la AnyTool, textbook grounding à la knowledge-augmented reasoning). The framework itself is largely prompt-pipeline engineering without new algorithms or theory.

Effect sizes over strong baselines are sometimes small: in chemistry, the gain over PoT is 2.7% and over ChemAgent 1.4% (GPT-4 and Llama settings show REFTOOL below RAG or PoT in places), and RAG baselines are competitive on physics (Table 12: PoT+RAG 65.1 vs REFTOOL 67.6), tempering the headline 12-13% claim which is driven mainly by comparisons against weaker tool-creation baselines.

Tool verification is self-referential: tools are validated only against LLM-generated demonstration examples and LLM-verified outputs, so factual errors in reference grounding can propagate; the paper acknowledges misinterpretation of nuanced concepts (chemistry) but the validation loop has no external ground-truth signal.

Framework presumes access to high-quality, domain-matched, well-structured reference materials (full textbooks); the method's applicability when references are noisy, incomplete, or partially wrong is untested, and the choice that no evaluation questions originate from the reference books is asserted but contamination screening procedures are not detailed.

Hyperparameters (nc, nt) are grid-searched on the SciBench validation set while other domains use defaults; also LATM baselines consume test-set instances for training/validation, creating slight setup asymmetries.

Human tool-quality evaluation relies on a single annotator per domain with limited sample sizes (50 tools, 20 questions), and the main-text ablation only covers causality and physics with single-turn reasoning.

strengths: The core idea — grounding automatic tool creation in external reference materials (textbooks, knowledge snippets) rather than the LLM's internal knowledge — is a sensible and clearly motivated direction, and the framework is described cleanly.

The evaluation is broad: three scientific domains, four utilization LLMs, multiple baseline families (tool creation methods, RAG, and domain-specific reasoners), plus a non-scientific XLR translation experiment with unstructured references.

Useful analyses beyond headline numbers: ablations isolating code-form tools vs. hierarchical selection, cost comparisons, human evaluation of tool quality along four dimensions, human-model tool selection consistency, and comparison against training/fine-tuning on the reference materials (Table 8), which is a thoughtful and non-trivial baseline.
The paper is generally well written, with reproducibility support (prompts in appendix, stated model versions, evaluation protocols consistent with original benchmarks).
weaknesses: The headline '12.3% / 13.0% improvement' is misleading framing: it is computed against weaker tool-creation baselines. Against the strongest and simplest baseline (PoT), the gains are much smaller and uneven — e.g., ~4.5 points on causality, ~2.6 points on physics, and ~2.7 points on chemistry on average, and for GPT-4 on chemistry the improvement is marginal (53.4 vs 51.8). The gains over well-engineered domain-specific methods (e.g., ChemAgent on Gemini-1.5-Pro) are similarly modest.

Results are inconsistent across models: in several settings REFTOOL underperforms the plain PoT baseline (e.g., GPT-4 on causality 38.7 vs 34.2 is positive, but GPT-4 in Table 4 ablations, and Hierarchical RAG sometimes beats REFTOOL, e.g., Gemini-1.5-Pro on physics 64.0 vs 58.8), suggesting the hierarchical-selection and code-form components do not reliably contribute, weakening the claimed mechanism-level conclusions.

Reference materials are hand-picked to exactly match each benchmark's domain (and sub-datasets with overlap are excluded). This domain-matching is a strong assumption of the method that limits the claimed generality, and no experiment tests robustness when the reference is only partially relevant or mismatched.

Limited novelty methodologically: the components (LLM tool/skill generation with execution-based validation, hierarchical retrieval mirroring AnyTool/Du et al., PoT/ReAct integration) are all well-established; the contribution is primarily the grounding of tool creation in reference text, which is a natural but incremental combination.

Tool verification relies on model-generated demonstration examples whose answers are themselves model-produced, so validation can confirm incorrect tools (self-consistency rather than correctness); the human evaluation samples only 50 tools per domain and does not measure downstream harm from subtly wrong tools.

Some experimental settings are favorable to the method: hyperparameters (nc, nt) are grid-searched on SciBench's validation set for chemistry while defaults are used elsewhere; datasets are small (e.g., SciBench sub-datasets), so several reported differences fall within plausible noise, and statistical significance is only reported in aggregate.

The abstract's breadth claim ('broadly generalizable') rests on a single non-scientific task (Zhuang translation) and one extra physics sub-dataset; the chrF++ gain over the strongest baseline (1.6 points) is small relative to the narrative.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: existing automatic tool-creation methods (LATM, Creator, TroVE) rely on the LLM's internal knowledge and fail in specialized domains; grounding tool creation in external reference material is a sensible and useful idea.

Comprehensive evaluation: three scientific domains (causality, physics, chemistry), four LLMs for utilization, multiple tool-creation and domain-specific baselines, plus RAG and fine-tuning comparisons; the fine-tuning comparison in Table 8 is a thoughtful additional baseline.
Good ablation design that separates the two claimed contributions (code-form tools vs. hierarchical selection), with Hierarchical RAG and similarity-retrieval variants isolating each component.

Strong generalization evidence: tool reusability on SciBench-fund, robustness to alternative tool-creation LLMs, and an ambitious non-scientific application (extremely low-resource Zhuang translation) demonstrating unstructured reference handling.

Useful analyses: human evaluation of tool quality (faithfulness, correctness, usefulness), tool-selection consistency with domain experts, and a cost analysis showing large efficiency gains over ChemAgent and Physics Reasoner.
Practical significance: tools are dataset-agnostic, amortized creation cost, and the framework degrades gracefully to standard PoT/ReAct when no tool applies.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the pipeline (LLM generates code tools from documents, validates them on self-generated examples, retrieves hierarchically) is a fairly natural combination of tool creation, RAG, and AnyTool-style hierarchical retrieval; the conceptual contribution is more an empirical finding than a new technique.

The headline 12.3%/13.0% improvement is measured against relatively weak tool-creation baselines; margins over the strongest baselines are much smaller (e.g., chemistry: 57.7 vs. ChemAgent 56.3 and PoT 55.0; physics: 54.8 vs. PoT 52.2), and in some model/dataset cells REFTOOL loses to plain PoT, so per-case gains are inconsistent.

A key practical assumption is under-examined: a human must select a high-quality, domain-matched reference textbook (an oracle-like resource). The paper does not discuss how reference quality/coverage affects performance or what happens with imperfect or partially relevant references.

Tool verification relies on self-generated examples whose gold answers come from the model itself; the human evaluation (50 tools/domain, reportedly one expert) cannot rule out systematic biases in examples that mask incorrect tools, and inter-annotator reliability is not reported.

Hyperparameter tuning (nc, nt) is performed via grid search only for chemistry, while causality/physics use defaults; the unequal treatment slightly weakens cross-domain comparability, and no variance or multiple-run analysis is reported for the main results despite significance claims.

Reference leakage concerns are only partially addressed: the 'atkins' SciBench sub-dataset is excluded due to overlap with the reference, but the extent to which textbook content overlaps with the remaining benchmarks' knowledge (formulas, constants) is not analyzed.
